name: Request Scheduling
question: Does this have to run now, and at full speed?
summary: Control when and how requests reach the model: queue them, merge identical requests already in flight, rate-limit per user, and move non-urgent work to quiet hours or cheaper service tiers. Smoother load also lets you size reserved capacity near the average instead of the peak.
useCases: Mixed workloads: interactive chat plus reports, indexing, enrichment
Provisioned or reserved capacity you pay for by the hour
Multi-tenant products that need fair use and spend limits

items.detail: run reports and indexing when demand is low
lower-priority tiers at a discount, where offered
reserved throughput sized to smoothed load

steps: Tag every request as interactive, near-real-time or background
Send background work through a queue with retries and backoff
Set per-tenant quotas and alerts on spend
Review utilization regularly and right-size reserved capacity
pitfalls: Queued work adds delay, so keep interactive paths separate
Retries without backoff multiply cost during outages
Hard quotas can block legitimate spikes; allow controlled bursts
remember: Urgent now. Everything else when it’s cheap.
caption: Same total work, lower peak. Reserved capacity only has to cover the peak.

steps.title: Tag every request
steps.text: Label each call interactive, near-real-time or background. Chat is interactive; end-of-day contract-note summaries are background.

steps.title: Give each class its own queue
steps.text: Separate queues and worker pools mean a bulk job can never sit in front of a customer’s chat message.

steps.title: Drop duplicates
steps.text: The same note is often enqueued twice by a retry or a double click. A Redis key with SET NX skips work already in flight or done.

steps.title: Retry with backoff and jitter
steps.text: On a 429, wait 1 s, 2 s, 4 s… plus a random fraction. Immediate retries during an outage multiply load and cost.

steps.title: Move background work off-peak
steps.text: The nightly job starts at 00:30, when chat traffic is lowest, instead of at 16:00 on top of the afternoon load.

steps.title: Right-size reserved capacity
steps.text: The peak falls from 11 units to the interactive peak of 8, so reserved capacity shrinks and utilization rises from 43% to 59%.

pros: Reserved capacity can be sized near the interactive peak, not the combined peak
Interactive users are protected from bulk jobs
Backoff prevents retry storms from multiplying cost during outages
cons: Queues, workers and schedules are more infrastructure to run
Hard quotas can block legitimate spikes
Priorities need ongoing tuning as traffic changes
avoidWhen: All traffic is interactive and must be served immediately
You pay purely per token with no reserved capacity and no rate-limit pressure (gains are small)

playgroundGuide.scenario: A broker runs live chat all day and, after market close, a job that summarizes contract notes for 200,000 clients. The job becomes available at 16:00 and must be ready by 08:00. You pay for reserved capacity by the hour, sized to the busiest hour. You decide when and how the job runs.
controls: Choose whether the job starts at 16:00 at full speed or goes through a priority queue that uses only spare capacity.
Drag the sliders to set reserved capacity and the job’s concurrency limit.
Tick the box to skip duplicate notes.

outputs.name: Hourly chart
outputs.meaning: Blue is chat, amber is the background job, the dashed line is reserved capacity.

outputs.name: Capacity utilization
outputs.meaning: All work done in the day ÷ capacity paid for (capacity × 24 hours).

outputs.name: Chat delayed
outputs.meaning: Unit-hours of chat demand above capacity: customers waiting.

outputs.name: Reports ready
outputs.meaning: When the job finishes. It must be before 08:00.

presets.name: Run at 16:00
presets.expect: The job lands on the afternoon load: peak 11 units, so capacity is 11 ($660 a day), utilization 43%. Reports ready at 20:00.

presets.name: Priority queue, still 11 units
presets.expect: Same capacity, chat served first: nothing changes yet except that chat is protected. Utilization is still 43%.

presets.name: Cut capacity to 8, no queue
presets.expect: The job still starts at 16:00, so chat is delayed by 8 unit-hours between 16:00 and 20:00.

missions.text: Run with 8 units of capacity, no chat delays and reports ready by 08:00.
missions.hint: Switch to the priority queue, then lower capacity to 8.

missions.text: At 8 units, have the reports ready by 21:00.
missions.hint: At 8 units the queue finishes at 21:30. Removing duplicates shortens the job.

missions.text: Keep chat free of delays but make the reports miss 08:00.
missions.hint: In the priority queue, set the concurrency limit to 1 unit: 16 hours × 1 is less than 24 unit-hours.

tools.best: Task queues with separate worker pools, rate limits, retries with backoff and scheduled runs.
tools.ex: An interactive queue with 32 workers and a background queue with 6, plus a nightly beat schedule at 00:30.
pros: Mature and widely used in Python stacks
Routing, retries and scheduling built in
cons: Rate limits are per worker, not global
Needs a broker such as Redis or RabbitMQ

tools.best: High-throughput event streams that decouple producers from LLM worker pools.
tools.ex: Stream 5 million catalogue updates overnight into an enrichment consumer group that scales with lag.
cons: Heavy to run for small workloads
Priorities and delays need extra design

tools.best: Simple managed queues with delayed delivery and dead-letter queues.
tools.ex: Queue background summarization jobs and let a Lambda consumer drain them at a fixed concurrency.
cons: No built-in priority within a queue

tools.best: Durable workflows with retries, timeouts and schedules for long multi-step LLM jobs.
tools.ex: A nightly workflow that fans out 200,000 summaries, retries failures with backoff and resumes after a crash.
cons: A cluster to run, or a paid cloud

tools.best: A lower-priced service tier for requests that can tolerate slower responses and occasional unavailability.
tools.ex: Send nightly enrichment calls with service_tier="flex" and retry with backoff when capacity is unavailable.
cons: Slower, and requests can be rejected when busy

goals: Explain why reserved capacity is sized to the peak, and how shifting work lowers it
Design separate queues, deduplication and backoff for LLM traffic
Calculate peak demand and utilization before and after shifting work

practice.scenario: A broker generates end-of-day contract-note summaries for 200,000 clients. Instead of running at 4 pm alongside live chat, the jobs go to a queue processed overnight with rate limits and retries, while live chat keeps its own reserved capacity.

industries.use: End-of-day reports and statements queued after market hours
Catalogue enrichment overnight, customer chat in real time
Per-tenant quotas so one customer’s bulk job can’t starve others

practice.analogy: Running the washing machine at night on a cheaper electricity tariff, while the kettle still boils on demand.

library.name: Celery
library.what: The standard Python task queue: separate queues, rate limits, retries with backoff and scheduled runs.

numericDrill.question: Interactive load peaks at 6 units. Background work adds 3 units per hour for 4 hours, currently during that peak. Move it to hours where interactive load is 1. What peak capacity do you now need?
numericDrill.answer: Peak drops from 6 + 3 = 9 to max(6, 1 + 3) = 6 units: a third less reserved capacity for the same work.

interview.question: How do you keep interactive latency low while heavy background jobs run?
interview.answer: Separate queues and worker pools, prioritize interactive traffic, schedule background work off-peak, and cap background concurrency so it can't use up shared rate limits.

interview.question: Why use exponential backoff on retries?
interview.answer: Immediate retries during an outage or rate limit multiply load and cost. Backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s… with jitter) spreads them out, lets the provider recover and avoids synchronized retry storms.

mistakes.mistake: Retrying immediately in a tight loop
mistakes.fix: Exponential backoff with jitter and a retry cap

mistakes.mistake: One shared rate limit for chat and batch jobs
mistakes.fix: Separate quotas and queues per workload

quiz.question: End-of-day report generation runs at 16:00 alongside live chat and sets the peak you reserve capacity for. What is the best move?
options: Move the reports to an off-peak queue overnight
quiz.explanation: Deferrable work moved to quiet hours stops adding to the peak.

quiz.question: Interactive load peaks at 10 units. A background job adds 4 units for 3 hours during that peak. If you move it to hours where interactive load is 2, what peak must you provision for?
quiz.explanation: The peak becomes max(10, 2 + 4) = 10 units, down from 14.

quiz.question: Which measures give fair use across tenants of a multi-tenant AI product? Select all that apply.
options: Separate queues for bulk and interactive work
One shared key with no limits
quiz.explanation: Limits, quotas and separate queues stop one tenant’s bulk job from starving the others.

quiz.question: Retries back off from 1 second and double each time, for up to 5 retries. What is the total wait if all 5 happen?
20% of catalogue-enrichment requests are duplicates created by retries and double submissions. What is the fix?
options: Run them on a larger model
Hash each request and skip ones already in flight or done
quiz.explanation: Deduplication removes work entirely, the cheapest saving there is.

quiz.question: A day’s work totals 120 unit-hours, and 10 units of capacity are reserved around the clock. What is the utilization?
During a provider incident, spend tripled because clients retried failed calls immediately and repeatedly. What is the fix?
options: Exponential backoff with jitter and a retry cap
quiz.explanation: Immediate retries create retry storms. Backoff spreads them out and a cap stops endless loops.

quiz.question: Which requests are good candidates for deferral to off-peak hours? Select all that apply.
options: Live chat with a customer whose SIM is blocked
quiz.explanation: Anything nobody is waiting on can be deferred. A blocked customer is waiting now.

quiz.question: You need Python task queues with separate worker pools, per-task rate limits and retries. Which tool fits?
quiz.explanation: Celery routes tasks to queues and supports rate limits, retries and scheduled runs.

quiz.question: A nightly job fans out 200,000 calls and must resume cleanly after a crash, with retries and timeouts. Which tool fits best?
quiz.explanation: Temporal runs durable workflows that survive crashes, with first-class retries and schedules.

quiz.question: Nightly enrichment calls can tolerate slow responses, but your code expects synchronous calls. Which OpenAI option lowers the price with a one-parameter change?
quiz.explanation: Flex processing trades slower, sometimes unavailable responses for a lower price, without switching to a batch workflow.

quiz.question: Patient chat and 50,000 discharge-summary jobs share one queue, and morning chat waits behind the jobs. What is the fix?
options: Separate queues and worker pools, with chat served first
quiz.explanation: Separate queues mean bulk work can never sit in front of a waiting patient.

quiz.question: Reserved capacity drops from 12 to 9 units at $3 per unit-hour. What is the saving over a 30-day month?
What are genuine downsides of request scheduling? Select all that apply.
options: Hard quotas can block legitimate spikes
Queue backlogs can hide failures without monitoring
It raises the price per token
quiz.explanation: Scheduling trades delay and operational complexity for lower capacity costs. It does not change token prices.

quiz.question: On exam-results day, a hard per-school quota blocks students from the results assistant. What is the better policy?
options: Allow controlled bursts above the quota, with alerts
quiz.explanation: Quotas should protect against abuse without blocking legitimate spikes.

quiz.question: 2,000 truck devices retry at exactly 1, 2 and 4 seconds after an outage and hit the API in synchronized waves. What is the fix?
options: Add random jitter to each delay
quiz.explanation: Jitter spreads clients out so they do not retry in lockstep.

quiz.question: Settlement summaries total 20 unit-hours of work. Data is ready at 01:00, and 4 units of spare capacity are available each hour from then. When does the job finish?
What does a priority queue in front of fixed reserved capacity do? Select all that apply.
options: Lets background work use spare capacity
Keeps the capacity you must reserve close to the interactive peak
quiz.explanation: Priorities protect users and fill idle capacity with deferred work. Token prices are unchanged.

quiz.question: Which requests belong on the interactive path? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Anything a client is waiting for, or that is time-critical, stays interactive. End-of-day summaries can wait.

quiz.question: A Celery task has rate_limit="60/m", and 4 workers consume its queue. What is the most that can run per minute?
quiz.explanation: Celery task rate limits apply per worker instance, not globally: 4 × 60 = 240 a minute.
